summary:
The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991 through the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct.

The criminal law retains an unequal age of consent. The sources record 16 years for opposite-sex acts and 18 years for same-sex acts.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, maritime marriage law provides that a marriage is void if between two men or two women, and in 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated that a same-sex marriage is void as a community standard. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 that he did not support same-sex marriage and in 2016 that a referendum would not legalize it, defining marriage as between a male and a female determined at birth. Same-sex households are denied the rights accorded to opposite-sex married couples.

The Constitution prohibition on discrimination does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving of protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition.

No broad anti-discrimination or anti-harassment law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. Discrimination on those grounds in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal, including discrimination in healthcare or education. There are no national hate-crime laws addressing violence directed at lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.

Official statements evidence hostility toward transgender people. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the exile of transgender people from the Bahamas, denounced the growing transgender community, urged financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island to ensure they stay out of the way, and pledged $1,000 toward relocation.

A gay visitor was violently targeted during a major tourist event. On 8 May 2017 The Tribune reported that Adrian Brown, aged 24, born in Jamaica and resident in the United States, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival early on Saturday, and that he sought charges.

Lethal violence against gay men has resulted in acquittals and unsolved cases. A defendant who killed a homosexual HIV-positive man in 2009 was acquitted after invoking a gay-panic defence. On 10 June 2010 the president of the Court of Appeal stated that a person is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent being the victim of a homosexual act. The accused in the 2007 killing of Harl Taylor was found not guilty. Nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved.

Police action and public protest have affected lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender social life and tourism. Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 but made no arrests because no crime had been committed, and the Ministry of Tourism later apologized to the cruise company. Church groups protested lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender tourist groups, including opposition to a 2004 cruise associated with Rosie O'Donnell and a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise. No exclusively gay bars or clubs exist, the Nassau scene is underground, and groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas.

Social conditions indicate a high level of disapproval. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations that treat homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence and immorality, and politicians have been reluctant to support lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender rights legislation publicly. Surveys recorded 85.5 percent strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage in 2015 with 10.6 percent approving, and over 84 percent strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12 percent positive. Due to lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequality and homophobia, many lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people keep sexual orientation or gender identity private.
tangentialFactors:
Statutory protection is narrow and indirect. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists sexual life as sensitive personal data.

The Communications Act 2009 empowers the Utilities Regulation and Competition Authority to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference.

Film censorship has restricted lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender related content. The Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, although the government overruled the attempt.

Religious mobilization has opposed lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender visibility in media. In September 2007 the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee in response to a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo.

Social penalties extend to public roles. In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian.
localsOnly:
Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the Bahamian Trans Lives Matter campaign in April 2016 and stated that no laws protect transgender and intersex Bahamians. Member Torri Culmer advocates against termination of transgender and intersex workers from their jobs.

A workplace protection was removed after adoption. A clause in a 2001 Employment Bill that banned workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation was removed shortly after passage.

The 2016 equality referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people, while marriage eligibility was framed as between a man and a woman with male and female determined at birth.

Lesbian, gay and bisexual citizens face no prohibition on service in the police, military or prison service. In May 1998 National Security Minister Frank Watson declared that those forces do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
Procedures for legal gender recognition or change of gender marker are not sourced in the inventory. The position for a visitor whose documents do not match gender presentation remains unresolved.

Entry and visa rules as applied to transgender visitors, and airport or port security screening practice as it risks outing, are not sourced. No finding on those procedures can be stated.

Law governing access to bathrooms or other sex-segregated facilities for transgender visitors is not sourced.

Access to gender-affirming care or HIV-related care for visitors is not sourced beyond the recorded absence of HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions. Whether care is banned, restricted or available to a short-term visitor remains unresolved.

Enforcement of the Communications Act codes and the practical effect of the Data Protection Act provision for a visitor are not sourced.
